UNIT 17: HUMAN SETTLEMENT

KEY THEME
- Settlement refers to where people live. Where people choose to live is decided by site, situation and the services they can use (function). Settlement can be rural or urban.

KEY TERMS
- Settlement: a place where people live, e.g. village, town or city. It can range from a single house to a large city.
- Urban: built-up areas such as towns and cities; in Ireland, places with populations over 1,500.
- Rural: countryside areas with few buildings and people; populations under 1,500.
- Hinterland: the area around a town or city that depends on it for resources and services.
- Logainmneacha: Irish placenames that describe features of the landscape or history of an area.
- Site: the actual physical location of a settlement, e.g. flat land near a river.
- Nodal point: a place where routes meet (roads, railways, paths).
- Situation: the location of a settlement in relation to other places, e.g. near roads or other towns.
- Function: the main job or purpose of a settlement, e.g. trading.
- Multifunctional: a place with many different functions and services.
- Ribbon development: buildings in a long line along a road.
- Dispersed settlement: homes spread out over a large area.
- Linear settlement: buildings in a line, usually along a road, river or coast.
- Nucleated settlement: a group of buildings clustered closely together.
- Commonage: shared land between local farmers, e.g. for sheep.
- Enurement clause: only a person with a long local connection and local housing need can get planning permission.
- Clachan: a cluster of farmhouses, linked to the old rundale system.
- Brownfield site: land previously built on but now derelict and unused.
- Brain drain: young, skilled, educated people leaving an area.
- Counter-urbanisation: people moving to live in the countryside and commuting to towns.

URBAN AND RURAL SETTLEMENT
- Urban settlement (over 1,500 people) provides a wide range of services to residents and its hinterland.
- Rural settlement (under 1,500) is in the countryside; houses stand alone or in small groups such as villages, with limited services.
- Tailte Eireann (TE) maps show placenames in Irish (in italics) and English. Irish placenames often give clues about origins.

SITE FACTORS
- Water source: rivers and lakes gave fresh water, fish, hydroelectric power for old mills and boat transport. Fords (shallow crossings) developed into bridging points.
- Nodal or bridging point: bridges became meeting places for trade; later roads and railways focused on them. Example: Ballina, Co. Mayo on the River Moy.
- Drainage: a dry-point site is near water but safe from flooding (good drainage).
- Altitude and relief: settlements avoid steep slopes and land above 200 m; flat land is easier for houses and roads. High land has more rain, stronger winds, colder winters and landslide risk.
- Aspect: the direction a slope faces. In the Northern Hemisphere south-facing slopes are warmer and brighter.
- Soils: fertile brown earth soils in the east and south of Ireland support the largest population centres; poor soils mean fewer, smaller settlements.
- Resources: Killybegs, Co. Donegal and Castletownbere, Co. Cork grew from fishing; Navan, Co. Meath grew because of Tara Mines, Europe's largest lead and zinc mine (world's ninth-largest zinc mine; over 85 million tonnes of ore since 1977; tunnels 150 m to 1,000 m deep).
- Defence: Celts built ringforts on high sites (e.g. Dun Aonghasa, Inis Mor); Vikings chose easily defended coastal sites such as Dublin on the Liffey; Normans built castles near rivers.
- The coast: most of Ireland's largest towns are on the coast, estuaries or sheltered bays for fishing and trade.

SITE IN IRISH PLACENAMES
- High ground: tulach (mound) as in Tulach Mor (Tullamore, 'large mound'); cnoc (hill), drom (ridge), ard (height), sliabh (mountain), mullach (summit). Example: Fethard (Fiodh Ard), Co. Tipperary.
- Flat land: cluain (plain) as in Cluain Tarbh (Clontarf, 'plain of the bulls'); clar, magh or ma, machaire.
- Other examples: Beal (river mouth) - Beal an Atha (Ballina); Cionn (headland) - Kinsale; Gort and Acha (field) - Gort, Aughamore; Muine (thicket) - Monivea; Ros (small wood) - Roscommon; Cor (hill); Corra (swamp) - Corrydavitt; Doiri (oak grove) - Derrybeg; Tra (beach) - Tralee; Cladach (shore) - The Claddagh.

SITUATION FACTORS
- Situation is where a settlement is relative to its surroundings and its proximity to other features. It decides how a settlement grows.
- Natural routeways: valleys and gaps through uplands gave easy access.
- Developed routeways: railways, roads and motorways help expansion. Example: Athenry, Co. Galway is growing due to the M6 motorway and the Galway-Dublin railway.
- Uplands: give shelter and defence but can stop expansion.
- Coast: towns can only expand inland.
- Surrounding landscape: good land gives food and raw materials for trade.
- Proximity to other settlements: Bray, Co. Wicklow has grown because it is near Dublin.

SITUATION IN IRISH PLACENAMES
- Ath means ford or crossing point: Athlone, Ballina, Baile Atha Cliath (Dublin), Droichead Atha (Drogheda, 'crossing point of the bridge'). These were lowest crossing points for trade.
- Other examples: Gleann (valley) - Glentogher; Abhainn (river) - Ballinahown; Eas (waterfall) - Ballysadare; Sliabh (mountain) - Slieveroe; Bearna (gap) - Barna; Bealach (way) - Ballaghaderreen; Ceim (pass) - Keimaneigh; Loch (lake) - Loughrea; Mara (sea) - Kinvara.

FUNCTIONS OF SETTLEMENT
- Function is the reason a settlement was built and the services it provides for residents and its hinterland. Functions change over time, e.g. defence is no longer needed. Modern towns are multifunctional.
- Main functions: religious (churches, monasteries, mosques); residential (houses, estates, apartments); recreational (pitches, golf, pools, marinas); industrial (factories, industrial estates); commercial (shops, offices, retail parks); educational (schools, universities); port (harbours, quays, ferry terminals); open space (parks, woodland, trails); transport/communications (roads, railways, airports); tourism (hotels, museums, viewpoints); services (garda stations, hospitals, fire stations, post offices).
- Example: aerial photo of Oughterard, Co. Galway shows many functions.

FUNCTION IN IRISH PLACENAMES
- Defence: dun, rath, lios, cathair, caiseal (fort); e.g. Dun Mor (Dunmore, 'large fort'), Lismore, Rathgar, Cahermore, Cashel. Caislean (castle) - Castlebar. Both (hut) - Bohola.
- Religion: cill and eaglais (church) - Cill Dara (Kildare, 'Dara's Church'), Ballynaheaglish; mainistir (monastery) - Monasterboice; earagail (oratory) - Errigal Keerogue; tearmann (sanctuary) - Termon.
- Seat of power: Sui Finn (Seefin, 'Fionn's Seat'). Industry: An Muileann gCearr (Mullingar, 'crooked mill'). Residence: Attymachugh ('place of the house of McHugh'). Caladh (landing place) - Ballinchalla. Uaran (spring) - Oranmore.

CASE STUDY: SITE AND SITUATION OF FOXFORD, CO. MAYO
- Site: on both sides of the River Moy on gently undulating lowland about 10 m above sea level; a dry-point site (no buildings upstream and downstream). River gave fresh water, fish and transport. Fertile alluvial soils on the floodplains suited farming. Flat land made building easy.
- Situation: a bridging point (G 269 041), making it a nodal point linking the N26, the R318 and a road to the south, aiding trade. Mountains to the southeast, northwest and northeast gave shelter and protection. Lough Cullen nearby attracts tourists.

CASE STUDY: CHANGES IN FUNCTION OVER TIME - GALWAY CITY
- Norman origins (defence, administration, trade): 1232 Anglo-Normans led by Richard Mor de Burgo built a castle at today's Druid Lane. Galway became a walled trading town; plots were leased for rent.
- 1271: Richard Og replaced the castle with the Hall of the Red Earl after a charter allowed taxing of traded goods; taxes paid for the walls. The wall had five gates with tolls.
- 1395: Richard II made Galway a royal borough. 1484: Richard III let citizens elect a mayor and corporation, making Galway a city.
- Market around Mainguard Street; St Nicholas' Church (1320) gave a religious function.
- Merchant era (from about 1400): 14 merchant families, the 'Tribes of Galway', grew wealthy through trade; commerce became the main function. Lynch's Castle and Blake's Tower. Religious orders: Dominicans (1488), Augustinians (1508), Jesuits (1620).
- English rule (from 1652, Cromwell): trade declined, but the Eyre family built a quay and dock at the Long Walk around 1750 (port function). Population grew from 6,000 to 20,000 between 1700 and 1800, many poor in slums. Merchants moved out to Eyre Square and Dominick Street. Walls fell into disrepair by 1750 and were gone by 1800 (defence lost).
- 19th century: courthouse at Newtownsmith; grain mills along the Corrib and warehouses; Persse family distilleries and breweries in the 1840s (industry). 1845 Queen's College (now University of Galway) gave an educational function; University College Galway in 1908. 1851 railway from Dublin plus the Railway Hotel (now the Hardiman) began the tourist function; Salthill grew as a seaside resort.
- Modern multifunctional city: 1967 first industrial estate at Mervue; 1971 Digital Equipment Corporation employed 1,200 directly and 1,300 indirectly, working with the university and RTC, creating a computer-literate workforce before closing in 1993. Now Boston Scientific, Medtronic, Hewlett-Packard, Cisco and others are the biggest contributors to the economy, thanks to an educated workforce and good communications.
- Tourism grew after Shannon Airport (1960s); helped by the M6 and M18 and Shannon and Knock airports. Festival city: Galway Races, Arts Festival, Cuirt, Baboro, Oyster Festival and more. Most tourists from Britain, Europe and North America.

RURAL SETTLEMENT PATTERNS (ON TE MAPS)
- Dispersed: houses far apart. On fertile land, farmhouses surrounded by farmland (low density). On infertile uplands with thin soils and commonage for sheep, houses reached by third-class roads or laneways.
- Linear (ribbon development): houses along roads. Causes: urban sprawl (cheaper land outside towns, people commute); services (electricity, broadband, water mains run along roads); property sites (landowners sell road-side plots; enurement clauses); scenic areas (houses parallel to coast or lake, often holiday homes).
- Councils discourage ribbon development and one-off housing because services are cheaper in towns and villages, and septic tanks can leak and pollute groundwater.
- Nucleated (clustered): houses around a central point. Clachans come from the rundale system before the Great Famine: land jointly held, split into infield (better land, where houses clustered) and outfield (poorer land for rough grazing). Also villages around services such as a church, school, shop, post office, pub or pitch.
- Absence of settlement: river floodplains (flood risk); uplands with steep slopes (isolated, costly roads, poor soil, harsh climate, landslides); special areas of conservation or woodland (e.g. the Burren, Co. Clare).

CHALLENGES FACING RURAL IRELAND
- A rural area is countryside where agriculture is the main land use, with population under 1,500 (CSO). In 2022, 37% of Ireland's population lived in rural areas.
- Older population: higher dependency ratios.
- Economic inequality: lower incomes, few jobs; reliance on small farms and forestry.
- Services and transport: long distances to healthcare, schools, shops and banks; closures raise travel costs.
- Public transport: poor, so most use cars; a barrier for young people and people with disabilities; more emissions.
- Social isolation: lack of services and activities; poor access to mental health services; loss of community spirit.
- Emigration and brain drain: young educated people leave, causing a cycle of rural decline (clubs and services close, so more leave).
- Economic uncertainty: Trump's tariffs on EU produce, the Russia-Ukraine war, Covid-19, Brexit, climate change. After Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, fertiliser, energy, grain and feed costs soared.
- Environmental issues: 40% of Ireland's emissions come from agriculture. EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) and Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) require farmers to cut emissions; carbon tax raises fertiliser costs, causing tension.
- Counter-urbanisation: one-off houses and ribbon development; commuting adds to sprawl and congestion.
- Rising land prices: locals cannot afford homes.

SUSTAINABLE RESPONSES: NATIONAL PLANS
- Rural planning aims to protect the environment and scenery, protect rural distinctiveness from suburban schemes and ensure sustainable land use.
- National Planning Framework (2018, updated 2025): built on National Strategic Outcomes (NSOs) based on the UN Sustainable Development Goals. Aims: strengthen rural communities; plan growth and renew small towns and villages; support rural jobs; improve connectivity (rural transport, high-speed broadband); coordinate investment. NSOs include compact growth, enhanced regional accessibility, strengthened rural economies and communities, sustainable mobility, a strong economy, a low-carbon climate-resilient society, amenity and heritage, sustainable water and waste management, and access to quality childcare, education and health services.
- National Development Plan: 116 billion euro. Targets: transport links between rural and urban areas; education and training; social inclusion especially for older people (e.g. Men's Sheds - first in Tipperary in 2009, over 450 by 2022, highest per population in the world in 2020); preserving scenic areas; more homes by upgrading derelict, brownfield and vacant sites rather than one-off housing. There are 19,000 to 20,000 derelict residential properties in Ireland (late 2025).
- Other responses in the sample answer: grants of up to 50,000 euro to renovate derelict buildings; rural broadband roll-out; subsidised Local Link bus services.

SUSTAINABLE RESPONSES: COUNTY DEVELOPMENT PLANS
- Under the Planning and Development Act (2000), councils must make development plans and update them every five years, guided by the NPF and NDP.
- Concerns: correct zoning of land; infrastructure (transport, energy, water, wastewater, waste); protecting scenery and heritage structures; sustainable settlement and transport, cutting emissions and managing flood risk; preventing pollution; housing for local needs.

CASE STUDY: GALWAY COUNTY DEVELOPMENT PLAN 2022-2028 (RURAL HOUSING)
- Four designated rural areas:
- 1. Rural metropolitan areas (strong urban pressure): near Galway City, e.g. Moycullen, Oranmore, Athenry; populations grew 2016-2022. Objective: steady population, development in small towns and villages on brownfield sites.
- 2. Structurally weak areas: little growth or decline, e.g. Williamstown; fewer services. Objective: allow housing demand within planning guidelines.
- 3. Landscape sensitivity: scenic beauty or fragile ecosystems, e.g. coastline west of Kinvara. Housing discouraged except for proven local need.
- 4. An Ghaeltacht: permission given to people who can prove they speak Irish, to protect language and culture. Udaras na Gaeltachta's An Ghaeltacht Ghlas helps business parks switch to renewable energy; wastewater investment; special areas of conservation for peatlands, pearl mussels and the Twelve Bens. As of 2026, the Joyce Country area of North Connemara is a UNESCO Geopark, boosting tourism.

CASE STUDY: GTEIC, AN TEARMANN, CO. DONEGAL (COMMUNITY INITIATIVE)
- Community and enterprise hub in a small Donegal Gaeltacht village near Gaoth Dobhair.
- High-speed broadband workspace: private offices, hot desks, co-working space and meeting rooms; community centre and creche.
- Co-working hub opened in 2018; joined the Connected Hubs Platform in 2021 (funded by the Western Development Commission).
- Thriving with remote workers; key benefit is social connection in a dispersed rural area.

rows.prompt: What population does a place need to be counted as urban in Ireland?
rows.explanation: Urban settlement refers to places with populations over 1,500.

rows.prompt: What is a hinterland?
options: The oldest part of a town inside its walls
A road that bypasses the centre of a town
The area around a town that depends on it for services
The highest point of land near a settlement
rows.explanation: The hinterland is the surrounding area that depends on a town or city for resources and services.

rows.prompt: What is the site of a settlement?
options: Its location compared with other towns
The actual land on which it is built
The main job or purpose of the town
The number of people who live there
rows.explanation: Site is the actual physical location, e.g. flat land near a river; situation is location relative to other places.

rows.prompt: What is a dry-point site?
options: Land that has no water supply nearby
A site on a high, dry mountain top
A site where a river has dried up
Land near water that is safe from flooding
rows.explanation: A dry-point site is along a river or lake where flooding is unlikely and it is safe to build.

rows.prompt: Why is a south-facing slope better for settlement in Ireland?
options: It is sheltered from all rain
It has the most fertile soils
It is closer to the coast
rows.explanation: In the Northern Hemisphere south-facing slopes receive warmer, brighter conditions.

rows.prompt: Which town grew because of Tara Mines?
rows.explanation: Navan, Co. Meath expanded due to Tara Mines, Europe's largest lead and zinc mine.

rows.prompt: Above what height do settlements tend not to be built?
rows.explanation: Settlements tend not to be built on steep slopes or land above 200 m.

rows.prompt: Where in Ireland are fertile brown earth soils and the largest population centres?
rows.explanation: Fertile brown earth soil is found in the east and south, where the largest population centres are.

rows.prompt: Why is Foxford, Co. Mayo described as a nodal point?
options: Its bridge links the N26 with other roads
It sits at the mouth of a large estuary
It was built on a high defensive hill
It has the largest market in Mayo
rows.explanation: The bridge over the Moy connects the N26, the R318 and a road to the south, making it a route focus.

rows.prompt: What does the Irish word 'tulach' mean in a placename?
rows.explanation: Tulach means a mound or elevated site, as in Tulach Mor (Tullamore, 'large mound').

rows.prompt: What does Cluain Tarbh (Clontarf) mean?
rows.explanation: Cluain means plain, so Cluain Tarbh means 'plain of the bulls'.

rows.prompt: What does the Irish word 'Ath' in placenames like Athlone tell us?
options: The town was built beside a castle
The town was built on a mountain pass
The town was built near a monastery
The town was built at a ford or crossing point
rows.explanation: Ath means ford or crossing point, showing a settlement founded at a river crossing.

rows.prompt: Which placename word shows a defence function?
rows.explanation: Lios, like dun, rath, cathair and caiseal, means fort.

rows.prompt: What does An Muileann gCearr (Mullingar) suggest about the town's original function?
rows.explanation: It means 'crooked mill', a place of industrial activity.

rows.prompt: What does 'multifunctional' mean?
options: A town that has changed its name
A village with one main street
A place with many functions and services
A city with more than one river
rows.explanation: Modern towns and cities are multifunctional, providing many services.

rows.prompt: Garda stations, hospitals and post offices are examples of which function?
rows.explanation: Services (civil or public services) include garda stations, hospitals, fire stations and post offices.

rows.prompt: Who established a castle in Galway in 1232?
rows.explanation: In 1232 the Anglo-Normans led by Richard Mor de Burgo built a castle at today's Druid Lane.

rows.prompt: Who were the 'Tribes of Galway'?
options: Norman soldiers who guarded the walls
rows.explanation: From about 1400, 14 merchant families who grew rich through trade became known as the Tribes of Galway.

rows.prompt: What event in 1851 began Galway's tourist function?
options: The arrival of the railway from Dublin
The building of the Long Walk quay
rows.explanation: The 1851 Dublin to Galway railway and the Railway Hotel started the tourist function, helped by Salthill.

rows.prompt: Why was Digital Equipment Corporation important to Galway?
options: It built the city's first university
It developed the port at the Long Walk
rows.explanation: Opened in 1971 and employing 1,200 directly, it created a skilled workforce that attracted other multinationals.

rows.prompt: What is ribbon development?
options: Houses spread far apart on farms
Houses built on a river floodplain
Houses built in a line along a road
rows.explanation: Ribbon (linear) development is buildings constructed in a long line along a road.

rows.prompt: Why do councils discourage one-off housing?
options: Houses in the countryside are too large to heat
Services cost more and septic tanks can pollute groundwater
Farmers need all rural land for growing crops
Roads in rural areas are too narrow for cars
rows.explanation: It is cheaper to service housing in towns, and individual sewage tanks can leak into groundwater.

rows.prompt: What was the rundale system?
options: A system of building houses along roads
A planning law for Gaeltacht areas
Farmland jointly held and split into infield and outfield
A scheme to build villages around churches
rows.explanation: In rundale, farmland was held jointly and split into infield and outfield; houses clustered as clachans.

rows.prompt: What is an enurement clause?
options: A rule that only local people with housing need can build
A rule that houses must face south
A ban on building near rivers
A grant to repair derelict houses
rows.explanation: It means only someone who has lived in the area a long time and has a local housing need can apply.

rows.prompt: Why is there an absence of settlement on river floodplains?
options: There is a risk of regular flooding
The soil is too poor for farming
The land is too steep for roads
The area is protected for wildlife
rows.explanation: Floodplains are left empty because of the risk of regular flooding.

rows.prompt: What percentage of Ireland's population lived in rural areas in 2022?
rows.explanation: In 2022, 37% lived in settlements under 1,500 or individual rural houses.

rows.prompt: What is the cycle of rural decline?
options: As farms grow, villages shrink and close
As people leave, services close and more people leave
As tourism grows, house prices rise
As roads improve, people stop using buses
rows.explanation: Brain drain leads to clubs and services closing, which causes more people to leave.

rows.prompt: Which event in 2022 caused fertiliser and feed costs to soar?
rows.explanation: When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, fertiliser, energy, grain and feed costs skyrocketed.

rows.prompt: What are the National Strategic Outcomes of the National Planning Framework based on?
rows.explanation: The NSOs are based on the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals.

rows.prompt: How often must county councils update development plans?
rows.explanation: Under the Planning and Development Act (2000), plans must be updated every five years.

rows.prompt: What is Gteic in An Tearmann, Co. Donegal?
options: A Men's Shed for older people
A UNESCO Geopark in the Gaeltacht
A community and enterprise hub with broadband
A rural bus service for isolated people
rows.explanation: Gteic provides workspace with high-speed broadband plus community facilities; it opened in 2018.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between the site and the situation of a settlement.
rows.model_answer: Site is the actual piece of land on which a settlement is built, for example flat, well-drained land near a river. Situation is where the settlement is in relation to its surroundings and other places, such as routeways, uplands, the coast or nearby towns. Situation decides how a settlement grows.

rows.prompt: Describe three site factors that attracted early settlers.
rows.model_answer: A water source such as a river gave fresh water, fish, power and transport. A dry-point site near water was safe from flooding. Flat, low land under 200 m with fertile soils was easy to build on and farm, and defensive sites such as hilltops gave protection.

rows.prompt: Using examples, explain how Irish placenames give evidence of function.
rows.model_answer: Words like dun, lios and rath mean fort, showing a defence function, e.g. Dunmore ('large fort'). Cill and eaglais mean church, showing a religious function, e.g. Kildare ('Dara's Church'). An Muileann gCearr (Mullingar) means 'crooked mill', showing an industrial function.

rows.prompt: Name five functions of a modern settlement.
rows.model_answer: Modern settlements can have residential, commercial, industrial, educational and religious functions. Others include recreational, port, transport, tourism, open space and services such as hospitals and garda stations.

rows.prompt: Briefly describe how Galway City's functions changed over time.
rows.model_answer: Galway began in 1232 as a Norman castle and walled town with defence, administration and trade functions. The merchant 'Tribes' made commerce dominant from about 1400. Under English rule the defence function was lost, while port, industry, education (1845) and tourism (railway 1851) grew. Today it is a multifunctional city with multinational industry and festivals.

rows.prompt: Name the four rural settlement patterns and give one reason for each.
rows.model_answer: Dispersed settlement occurs where farmhouses are surrounded by their farmland. Linear settlement occurs along roads because services like electricity and broadband run there. Nucleated settlement clusters around services or as old clachans. Absence occurs on floodplains, steep uplands or protected areas.

rows.prompt: Describe two challenges that young people face in rural Ireland.
rows.model_answer: There are limited job opportunities and lower incomes, so many young, educated people leave in a brain drain. Poor public transport means they rely on cars, which limits access to education, work and social activities.

rows.prompt: Describe the four designated rural areas in the Galway County Development Plan 2022-2028.
rows.model_answer: Rural metropolitan areas near Galway City, like Oranmore, face strong urban pressure, so development is focused on villages and brownfield sites. Structurally weak areas like Williamstown are declining, so housing demand is facilitated. Areas of landscape sensitivity, like west of Kinvara, discourage housing. In the Gaeltacht, permission is given to people who can speak Irish.

rows.prompt: Explain how Gteic helps the people of An Tearmann, Co. Donegal.
rows.model_answer: Gteic is a community and enterprise hub that gives workers and entrepreneurs office space with high-speed broadband, so people can work remotely without leaving the area. It also has a community centre and creche. Workers value the social connection in a dispersed rural area.

rows.prompt: With reference to one Irish settlement you have studied, explain how its site and situation helped it to develop. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Foxford, Co. Mayo developed on both sides of the River Moy on gently undulating lowland about 10 m above sea level. It is a dry-point site, as there are no buildings upstream and downstream where flooding may occur. The river gave early settlers fresh water, fish and transport. Fertile alluvial soils on the floodplains made it ideal for farming, and the flat land made building roads and houses easy. Its situation is a bridging point over the Moy, making it a nodal point linking the N26, the R318 and a road to the south, which helped trade. Mountains to the southeast, northwest and northeast gave shelter and protection, and nearby Lough Cullen attracts tourists who boost the local economy.
rows.marking_scheme: Named settlement 2m. 9 SRPs x 2m, covering both site and situation (max 6 SRPs on either). Map/grid references may count as SRPs. Max 20 marks.

rows.prompt: Examine how the functions of an Irish urban settlement have changed over time. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: Galway City shows how functions change. In 1232 Richard Mor de Burgo built a castle at Druid Lane for defence and administration, and Galway became a walled trading town. In 1271 the Hall of the Red Earl became the administrative centre, collecting taxes to build walls with five toll gates. In 1484 it became a city with its own mayor. St Nicholas' Church (1320) and the Dominicans, Augustinians and Jesuits gave a religious function. From about 1400 the 14 merchant 'Tribes of Galway' made commerce the main function, shown by Lynch's Castle. After Cromwell in 1652 trade fell, but the Eyre family built a quay at the Long Walk around 1750, keeping a port function. The walls disappeared by 1800 as defence was lost. In the 19th century mills on the Corrib and the Persse breweries gave an industrial function, Queen's College (1845) an educational function, and the 1851 railway and Railway Hotel a tourist function. Today Galway is multifunctional: Mervue industrial estate (1967), Digital (1971) and now Boston Scientific and Medtronic, plus festivals such as the Galway Races.
rows.marking_scheme: Named settlement 2m. Examination: 14 SRPs x 2m. Must show change over time (at least two eras). Dates, named buildings and companies count as SRPs. Max 30 marks.

rows.prompt: Describe and explain two rural settlement patterns found on Irish Ordnance Survey (TE) maps. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Linear or ribbon settlement is where houses are built in a line along roads. It happens because of urban sprawl, as land near towns is expensive and people live along approach roads and commute. Electricity, broadband and water mains run along roads, so sites there have easy access to services. Landowners sell road-side plots due to housing demand, and houses are built parallel to coasts or lakes for scenic views, often as holiday homes. Nucleated settlement is where houses cluster closely around a central point. Clachans are clusters of farmhouses dating from the rundale system before the Famine, when land was split into infield, where houses were built, and outfield for grazing. Villages also cluster around services such as a church, school, shop, post office or pub.
rows.marking_scheme: Pattern 1 named 2m + 4 SRPs x 2m. Pattern 2 named 2m + 4 SRPs x 2m. Max 20 marks.

rows.prompt: Examine how the challenges facing rural settlements in Ireland are being responded to in a sustainable way. Refer to local and national responses. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: Rural Ireland faces an older population, lower incomes, few jobs and a brain drain of young people, causing a cycle of rural decline as services such as post offices close. Poor public transport causes social isolation. Nationally, the National Planning Framework (2018, updated 2025) aims to strengthen rural communities, renew small towns and villages and improve rural transport and broadband. The National Development Plan invests 116 billion euro in rural-urban transport links, education, social inclusion and more homes on derelict, brownfield and vacant sites instead of one-off housing. Grants of up to 50,000 euro help renovate derelict buildings, high-speed broadband allows remote working, and subsidised Local Link buses reduce isolation. Men's Sheds improve social inclusion. Locally, the Galway County Development Plan 2022-2028 directs growth in rural metropolitan areas like Oranmore onto brownfield sites, protects sensitive landscapes west of Kinvara and gives Gaeltacht permission to Irish speakers. An Ghaeltacht Ghlas helps business parks switch to renewable energy. In An Tearmann, Co. Donegal, Gteic, opened in 2018, provides broadband workspace, a community centre and a creche, giving remote workers social connection.

rows.prompt: With reference to examples, describe how Irish language placenames provide evidence of the site, situation and function of settlements. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Placenames give clues to site. Tulach means mound, so Tullamore was built on a large mound; cnoc, drom and ard also show high ground. Cluain means plain, so Clontarf ('plain of the bulls') was built on flat land, and Tra in Tralee shows a beach site. Placenames also show situation. Ath means ford, so Athlone, Dublin (Baile Atha Cliath) and Drogheda were founded at river crossing points used for trade. Bearna (gap) in Barna and Loch in Loughrea show a pass or lakeside situation. Placenames show function too. Dun, lios and rath mean fort, as in Dunmore and Lismore, showing defence. Cill means church, as in Kildare, showing a religious function, and Mullingar ('crooked mill') shows industry.
